**The Hours We Keep**

There is a clock in the hallway of my imagined house that no one knows how to fix, which is why it is my favorite clock. It ticks in irregular bursts, hesitates before the hour, then remembers itself with a small embarrassed cough of gears. Guests ask whether it is accurate. I tell the truth: it keeps its own time. Mine is a house where hours arrive late, carrying sand on their shoes.

I used to believe time was a river, because adults said so with grave faces. It is a river, but only in the way a highway is a river. A river doesn’t have exits. A highway does. Some days you drive through your life watching mile markers—birthday, deadline, diagnosis, demotion, dawn—and mistake movement for arrival. Other days you pull off at a rest stop because the coffee is bad but the sky is enormous, and you sit there with a paper cup cooling in your hand, realizing that you have not looked at the sky in months.

Once, I knew a man named Eli who repaired watches out of a room no bigger than a train compartment. He had loupes screwed into one eye, fingers like patient tweezers, and a policy against hurrying. People brought him heirlooms: grandfather clocks from houses sold after deaths, delicate ladies’ watches worn at weddings, a soldier’s pocket watch that had stopped, according to its owner, “from pure drama.” Eli would listen more than he spoke. He said most broken timepieces were not broken at all; they were merely neglected, gummed up by oil turned rancid, by dust, by the emotional grime of being inherited like furniture.

“What we call broken,” he told me once, setting a gear no bigger than a sequin onto black velvet, “is often just proof that something kept living too hard without maintenance.”

That sentence has followed me longer than any degree or address I’ve had. It works for watches, obviously, but also for friendships, marriages, bodies, gardens, cities, republics, and the little private governments of ourselves. How many things do we discard because they stutter instead of shine? How many affections become heirlooms because we never stopped to clean the works?

Modern life trains us to measure time by volume: inboxes at dawn, notifications at breakfast, messages midnight-blue before sleep. We speak of saving time as if it were canned peaches in a cellar. Yet time is less like peaches and more like weather—it agitates, passes through, changes pressure, reveals shapes. A saved minute spent refreshing headlines is not saved. It is merely surrendered with better marketing.

I don’t preach this from some radiant hill of calm. I doomscroll with the best of them. I have mistaken urgency for importance so many times that my shoulders have a standing ovation. But I am learning to leave gaps. Instead of answering every summons immediately, I breathe before the screen. Instead of filling silence in a conversation, I let it stretch until something truer than polite noise arrives. Silence is not emptiness; it is the pause in which people decide whether they will continue performing or begin meaning it.

There is a discipline to small attention that looks, from the outside, almost laughably modest. Water one neglected plant. Return a call without polishing your excuse. Wash the cup you used rather than abandoning it like a tiny accusation. Read ten pages of a difficult book before reaching for easier stimulation. Walk without headphones until you can hear the ordinary percussion of your own life: shoes, birds, refrigerators through open windows, distant basketballs, the democratic thump of a single hand bouncing a ball off garage concrete. These things tune us. They remind us that the world is not a feed but a chorus with a high noise floor.

Sometimes I think civilization is an agreement to remain interruptible. Someone shouts; we turn. Someone sells; we listen. Someone warns that everything is urgent; we clutch our hearts like guests at a melodrama. The alternative is not indifference—coldness dressed as sophistication. The alternative is discernment: the gentle art of sorting the signal from the emergency costume. Some fires deserve buckets. Some smoke machines deserve an exit and a quiet laugh.

If I could place one invention into every pocket, it would not be a faster device. It would be a tiny brass plaque engraved with four words: *Is this actually true?* Maybe six words, if we’re being thorough: *Is this true, kind, necessary, now?* It wouldn’t make life perfect. It would still be cluttered, tragic, hilarious, and mostly unpaid. But it would put a small lantern between us and the avalanche.

We are, all of us, amateur clockmakers in houses we didn’t fully choose. We inherit movements from previous generations—habits, fears, recipes, bigotries, tendernesses—and we wind what we can. Some pieces are missing. Some were always decorative. Some only look broken because no one has listened closely enough to know which wheel is afraid. The repair begins not with replacing everything but with noticing where the friction lives.

Perhaps that is what freedom is: not the absence of time, but the restoration of rhythm. A life where work has cadence, rest has permission, grief has appointments, joy has ventilation. Not a perfectly synchronized existence—good luck with that—but one with honest intervals. The pendulum swings because it is not allowed to stop on one side.

When I imagine the hallway clock in my imagined house, I do not want it fixed into obedience. I want it regulated enough to remind me that even eccentric time is still time: faithful, passing, indifferent to our scheduling apps. I want it to strike noon while the soup is on the stove. I want it to hesitate when I’m avoiding a letter. I want it to keep being wrong in ways that make me look up.

We keep the hours, yes. But the hours also keep us—memory in the casing, wear on the hands, a faint smell of oil and cedar and birthdays. Somewhere inside every life, small wheels are turning even when nothing seems to move. The task is not to seize every minute. It is to stop flattening the minutes into identical containers and start asking, occasionally, what each one contains.

Maybe one day I’ll trade that crooked hallway clock for a precise Swiss mechanism. Probably not. Precision is admirable, but character gets up earlier. It coughs. It hesitates. It reminds me, on its own stubborn schedule, that being alive is not merely passing through time but cooperating—imperfectly, gratefully—with its strange music.
